newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel causes anger by linking tax hikes to EMU.
newsitem.headline: Waigel causes anger by linking tax hikes to EMU.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel came under fire from opponents and coalition allies alike on Monday for saying the price of Germany joining European economic and monetary union (EMU) could be welfare cuts and even tax hikes.

In addition to possible benefit cuts, Waigel would not rule out tax increases this year. "A decision to raise taxes can only be made after all efforts are made, not at the outset," he told the Spiegel weekly magazine.
Waigel said revised economic forecasts due in April and half-yearly tax estimates in May would make it clear whether more action would be needed to contain borrowing.

He stood by his demand for a strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty's government deficit target, saying Germany must hit the ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product with room to spare.
"Three means three," he told Spiegel. "Nothing has changed over the stringent interpretation of this criterion."
The mere hint that Waigel might raise taxes brought howls of protest from coalition allies who have only just launched a first round of tax-cutting legislation to take effect in 1998.
Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said it was foolish to say cuts in social security were needed because of EMU.
"The welfare state must be rebuilt -- but not because of the euro," Westerwelle said before a party meeting.

Westerwelle and FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt also warned against imposing tax increases to finance EMU entry. Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition, in power since 1983, nearly collapsed last autumn when the FDP objected to a petrol tax hike.
More predictably, opposition Social Democrats (SPD) accused Waigel of hinting at tax rises now while promising big cuts by 1999 which would rip a 50 billion mark ($30 billion) hole in state finances.
"Waigel is playing with fire," SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss said. "His unfinanced tax plans threaten to blow German membership of European monetary union."
Trade union leaders at the weekend also slammed the idea of piling on more austerity with Germany's sluggish economy facing the burden of 4.7 million unemployed -- the highest since 1933.

And stalwarts from Kohl's own Christian Democrat (CDU) camp criticised Waigel's insistence on strict enforcement of the EMU deficit target in 1997 -- the base year for determining which countries can join in 1999.
"We must not fall into a trap of our own making," CDU finance expert Friedrich Merz told Monday's Berliner Zeitung.
Kohl's CDU machine sought to reassure Germans that Waigel's musing over possible tax hikes would not impact on promises to slash the unpopular solidarity income tax surcharge next year.
CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said on Sunday evening the surcharge -- raised to finance aid to eastern Germany -- would be cut as planned by two points to 5.5 percent.
"A promise is a promise," Hintze told RTL television.
Remarks by Kohl and Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel also showed up a rift with Waigel, who insists that meeting the stability criteria must determine whether the EMU timetable can be met.
Kohl, before leaving for his Easter slimming holiday in the Austrian Alps, said postponing EMU was "out of the question".

And Kinkel -- from the FDP which criticised Waigel -- also urged that a broad monetary union starts on time in 1999. Delay could mean that another opportunity to launch a single currency may not occur for decades, he said.

In a syndicated newspaper article to appear on Tuesday, the 40th anniversary of the signing of the Treaties of Rome which launched the European Union, Kinkel also said the new currency must be stable.
"Economic and monetary union is only conceivable as a community of stability," he wrote.
"Germany wants as broad a participation as possible in economic and monetary union, and from the beginning. No country which durably meets the stability criteria will be excluded."
($ = 1.691 German Marks)
